intro: Prokofiev’s Piano Sonata No. 2, Op. 14, heard complete, has four movements: Allegro ma non troppo, Scherzo, Andante and Vivace. A tune from the first movement returns in the finale, a fast tarantella.

sections.label: A · Allegro: duplets over triplets
sections.mNote: Paired melody notes above triplet arpeggios.

sections.label: B · Scherzo: short phrases, repeated piano chords
sections.mNote: Repeated piano chords and clipped accents.

sections.label: C · Andante: melody over rocking bass
sections.mNote: A long melody above a slower accompaniment.

sections.label: D · Vivace: tarantella finale
sections.mNote: Fast tarantella figuration, interrupted by an earlier theme.

relations.label: The scherzo’s opening returns
relations.basis: The second movement has an A–B–A design; the matched later passage follows its contrasting middle. The movement boundary near 350 s is approximate, so the first excerpt begins slightly before that editorial marker. Formal outline: https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html. CENS diagonal mean 0.975, sustained 30 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 71.5 s (cache/form/prokofiev-piano-sonata-2.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The Andante phrase returns
relations.basis: The third movement restores its first lyrical section after a contrasting, more layered middle. These excerpts compare the expanding phrase in the two outer sections, as described in Emilia Zanetti’s account at https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html. CENS diagonal mean 0.949, sustained 26.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 119 s (cache/form/prokofiev-piano-sonata-2.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: An earlier melody returns in the finale
relations.basis: The finale recalls the first movement’s cantabile material. The measured pair crosses those movements and agrees with this cyclic recollection, documented at https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html. CENS diagonal mean 0.940, sustained 18 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 691 s (cache/form/prokofiev-piano-sonata-2.txt, candidate 5; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: First theme, duplets against triplets
cues.text: The right hand groups its melody in pairs over triplet arpeggios in the left. A percussive passage follows, and then the opening theme returns.
cues.evidence: Emilia Zanetti, Santa Cecilia programme note, 12 March 1965: the first theme’s duple figure and triplet arpeggios frame a percussive central passage. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second subject in 3/4
cues.text: A faster bridge, Più mosso in 2/4, leads to Tempo primo in 3/4 and the second idea, marked p. Zanetti called it sweetly lyrical and noted that the development dwells on it.
cues.evidence: First edition (Jurgenson plate 36673; Muzgiz reprint scanned at IMSLP), p. 4: Più mosso in 2/4, then Tempo primo in 3/4, marked p. Zanetti’s Santa Cecilia programme note (12 March 1965) describes the bridge and the quiet, sweetly lyrical second idea, on which the development lingers (translation ours): https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Origins of the sonata
cues.text: Prokofiev built the sonata partly from earlier music. An earlier sonatina became the first movement, and a piece written for Lyadov’s composition class became the scherzo. He added the Andante and finale in 1912.
cues.evidence: Zanetti’s Santa Cecilia programme note traces the sonata’s construction through Prokofiev’s autobiography and Israel Nestyev’s biography. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html

cues.title: Recapitulation
cues.text: The development ends fpp, and the recapitulation alters the opening bars only slightly. The faster bridge returns marked pp, then the 3/4 second idea, pp dolce. A later phrase is marked tristemente (sadly).
cues.evidence: First edition (Jurgenson plate 36673; Muzgiz reprint scanned at IMSLP), pp. 8–10: the development ends fpp, molto legato; in the recapitulation the Più mosso bridge is marked pp, the 3/4 idea Tempo primo, pp dolce, and a later phrase tristemente. Zanetti’s Santa Cecilia programme note: the recapitulation modifies only the profile of the opening bars and is almost entirely pianissimo before the concluding crescendo (translation ours): https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sabaneyev on the First Concerto, 1912
cues.text: In the summer of 1912 Prokofiev played his First Piano Concerto in Moscow, and the public received it warmly. The critic Leonid Sabaneyev called it harsh and coarse, primitive and cacophonous. The Second Sonata dates from the same year; the printed score gives 1912.
cues.evidence: Leonid Sabaneyev’s review in Golos Moskvy (1912), quoted with the Moscow première of summer 1912 and its success with the public in a Russian article on the Concerto (Yuzhno-Rossiiskii muzykalnyi almanakh, 2011; translation ours): https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/prokofiev-kontsert-1-dlya-fortepiano-s-orkestrom . The Sonata’s date, 1912, is printed in the first edition (Jurgenson plate 36673; IMSLP).

cues.title: Scherzo, Allegro marcato
cues.text: The scherzo is marked Allegro marcato, meaning fast, with the notes clearly struck. Short phrases sound against repeated chords. The pace slackens in the middle section, and then the opening section returns.
cues.evidence: The movement marking is listed in the IMSLP work catalogue. Zanetti describes the ABA form and more flexible middle section; Arrigo Quattrocchi identifies the repeated chords. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Andante, melody over rocking bass
cues.text: The Andante opens with a rocking bass under a long melody. The melody expands over the repeated bass figure, and a contrasting middle section follows.
cues.evidence: Zanetti’s note describes the Andante’s rocking bass, expanding melody and contrasting middle section. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Maximilian Schmidthof
cues.text: Prokofiev dedicated the sonata to Maximilian Schmidthof, a friend and fellow student at the St Petersburg Conservatory. Schmidthof took his own life in 1913, before the sonata was first played in 1914.
cues.evidence: The printed score (Jurgenson plate 36673; Muzgiz reprint scanned at IMSLP) is headed with the dedication to Maximilian Anatolyevich Schmidthof: https://imslp.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No.2,_Op.14_(Prokofiev,_Sergey) . A fellow student at the Conservatory, he killed himself in 1913, before the Moscow première of 1914: https://www.belcanto.ru/prokofiev_ps2.html and https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/prokofiev-sonata-2-dlya-fortepiano (Russian).

cues.title: Andante, middle section
cues.text: In the middle section of the Andante, a chromatic inner line moves in semitones between the melody and the bass, while the upper voice moves in longer phrases. For a few bars the accompaniment changes to an uneven seven-quaver measure.
cues.evidence: Zanetti identifies the upper melody, chromatic inner line and brief 7/8 passage in the Andante’s second section. The existing cue places this discussion within the slow movement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Prokofiev’s autobiography, 1941
cues.text: In his autobiography of 1941, Prokofiev placed the lyrical side of his music ahead of its toccata-like drive. He recalled how little attention critics had paid to the melodies of his youth.
cues.evidence: Simon Morrison, preface to Henle HN 1581 (2023), p. IV, discussing Prokofiev’s 1941 autobiography. https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: Finale, tarantella
cues.text: The finale is a tarantella in quick groups of three. A leaping episode with sharp accents breaks into the running notes, and the cantabile second theme of the first movement returns briefly. The tarantella then continues to the end.
cues.evidence: Zanetti identifies the tarantella rhythm, leaping episode and return of the first movement’s cantabile theme. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Finale, perpetual motion
cues.text: The finale is a perpetual motion, with a tightly pulsing rhythm under a sharp, ironic theme high on the keyboard. Arrigo Quattrocchi called it the high point of the sonata and a prototype, perhaps unequalled, of many similar pages by Prokofiev.
cues.evidence: Arrigo Quattrocchi’s programme note (Accademia Filarmonica Romana, Teatro Olimpico, Rome, 8 February 1989) on the Vivace finale. Translation ours. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html

cues.title: First performance, Moscow, 1914
cues.text: Prokofiev gave the first public performance of the sonata in Moscow on 5 February 1914. Jurgenson had published it the previous year. At the time the composer was still a student at the St Petersburg Conservatory.
cues.evidence: IMSLP documents the première, pianist and 1913 publication: https://imslp.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No.2,_Op.14_(Prokofiev,_Sergey). Prokofiev’s Conservatory studies run to 1914.

transitions.title: From first movement to Scherzo
transitions.to: B · Scherzo: short phrases, repeated piano chords
transitions.how: The first movement ends in D minor. The Scherzo is a separate movement, marked Allegro marcato. It opens with short accents and repeated chords in the piano. The first movement’s singing line and triplet arpeggios are replaced by short rhythmic phrases in both hands.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Sonata No. 2, movements I–II. The movement markings are listed by IMSLP; Zanetti and Quattrocchi describe their contrasting piano writing at https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html .

transitions.title: From Scherzo to Andante
transitions.from: B · Scherzo: short phrases, repeated piano chords
transitions.to: C · Andante: melody over rocking bass
transitions.how: The Scherzo, a short movement built on repeated chords and brief figures, ends before the Andante begins. In the Andante the piano plays a slower rocking bass, and a long melody rises above it. The upper voice holds its notes while the harmony changes several times beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Zanetti’s Santa Cecilia programme note describes the Scherzo’s brief figures and the Andante’s melody over a rocking bass. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html

transitions.title: Andante to Vivace tarantella
transitions.from: C · Andante: melody over rocking bass
transitions.how: The Andante ends, and the finale is marked Vivace. Fast groups of three take the place of the Andante’s longer notes. Both hands play the tarantella together, and leaps and accents cut across its running figures.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Sonata No. 2, movements III–IV; the Vivace marking is listed in the IMSLP catalogue. Zanetti describes the tarantella and leaping figures: https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html .

composer.born: 27 April (15 April Old Style) 1891; Prokofiev himself gave 23 April, Sontsovka, Ukraine, then Russian Empire
composer.epithet: Twentieth-century composer known for Romeo and Juliet, with its writing for strings, and for his piano music.
facts: Glière at Sontsovka, 1902–03; St Petersburg Conservatory, 1904–14
Russia · United States · Bavaria · Paris; settled in Moscow in 1936
The Love for Three Oranges · Romeo and Juliet · Cinderella · War and Peace
Seven symphonies, five piano concertos and nine completed piano sonatas

quote.text: It seemed to me that if Haydn had lived into our own time, he would have kept his way of writing while taking in something new.
quote.source: Prokofiev, short Autobiography (1941), recalling the summer of 1917; our translation

composer.background:
At Sontsovka, the Ukrainian estate his father managed, Prokofiev grew up hearing his mother play Beethoven and Chopin. She wrote down his first piano pieces; the earliest, an Indian Galop, dates from 1896. After a trip to the Moscow opera in 1900, the eight-year-old set about writing an opera of his own, The Giant, for the family to perform at home. His mother eventually stopped playing when she saw that he had overtaken her. Sergei Taneyev recommended proper lessons, and Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka teaching the boy, who was already filling manuscript books.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen, bringing four operas, two sonatas, a symphony and piano pieces to the entrance examination. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Lyadov harmony and counterpoint; later Anna Esipova took charge of his piano playing. Nikolai Tcherepnin taught conducting and encouraged his taste for Haydn and Mozart. His fellow student Nikolai Myaskovsky became the friend to whom he sent scores and complaints for the rest of his life. In December 1908 Prokofiev played some of his first distinctive pieces, Suggestion diabolique among them, at St Petersburg’s Evenings of Contemporary Music. The following spring his examination pieces shocked Lyadov, who heard Scriabin in them. In the final piano competition of 1914, with Esipova ill, Prokofiev played his own First Concerto. Glazunov opposed him, but Prokofiev was awarded the Rubinstein Prize, which was a grand piano.
